cards.title: 1.1.1 Measuring the Rate of a Chemical Reaction
body: The phrase “rate of reaction” means how fast the reaction is occurring or the speed of the reaction.

The rate of a reaction can be measured either in terms of how much of a reactant is being used up per unit of time or in terms of how much of a product is being formed per unit of time, depending on which is easier to do as the reaction proceeds.
The rate will then be measured by reading the volume of gas collected per unit of time.
The rate of a given reaction is not always the same.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the forward reaction of a system in equilibrium is endothermic, increasing the temperature of the system will:

options.A: Shift the equilibrium to the left.
options.B: Shift the equilibrium to the right.
options.C: Decrease the rate of the forward reaction.
options.D: Have no effect on the equilibrium constant $$K_c$$.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Treat heat as a reactant or product**
For an endothermic reaction, heat is absorbed: $$\text{Reactants} + \text{Heat} \rightleftharpoons \text{Products}$$.

**Step 2: Apply Le Chatelier's Principle**
Increasing temperature is equivalent to adding heat to the reactant side.

**Step 3: Predict the shift**
To consume the added heat, the system shifts to the **right** (towards products).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following parameters cannot be used directly to monitor the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.A: The volume of gas evolved over time.
options.B: The loss of mass of the reaction flask on a balance.
options.C: The total molecular mass of the inert nitrogen atmosphere above the reaction.
options.D: The change in color intensity of a transition metal ion solution.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand how rate is measured**
To measure rate, we must track a changing property of reactants or products over time.

**Step 2: Evaluate options**
Option A (volume of gas) changes as product gas forms. Option B (mass loss) changes as gas escapes. Option D (color intensity) changes as concentration of colorful species changes.

**Step 3: Analyze the inert gas**
The inert nitrogen gas above the reaction does not participate in the chemical reaction, so its properties remain constant and cannot monitor reaction rate.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The correct option is **C**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A chemical system reaches dynamic equilibrium when:

options.A: The concentrations of reactants and products are exactly equal.
options.B: The reactants are entirely converted into products and the reaction stops.
options.C: The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
options.D: The activation energy of the forward reaction becomes zero.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the definition of equilibrium**
Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state. This means the reactions do not stop, but rather occur in both directions simultaneously.

**Step 2: Compare rates**
At equilibrium, the forward rate of reaction equals the reverse rate of reaction.

**Step 3: Analyze concentrations**
Because the rates are equal, the net concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, but they are not necessarily equal in value.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The correct choice is **C**.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Chemical Equilibrium and Its Characteristics
body: A chemical reaction may be either reversible or irreversible.
A reversible reaction is one in which the reactants can form the products, and the products can also form the reactants under the conditions of the reaction.
As time passes and the reaction proceeds, the concentration of A and B will decrease whereas that of C and D will increase.
Since a decrease in concentration of the reactants reduces the rate of a reaction, the forward reaction rate will be decreasing with time.

cards.title: The law of mass action, step by step
body: **Law of mass action** (Guldberg and Waage, 1864): at constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the molar concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.
**Step 1 — Write both rates** for \(a\text{A} + b\text{B} \rightleftharpoons c\text{C} + d\text{D}\):
$$\text{rate}_f = k_f[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b \qquad \text{rate}_b = k_b[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d$$
**Step 2 — At equilibrium the two rates are equal:** \(k_f[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b = k_b[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d\).
**Step 3 — Collect the constants on one side:**
$$K_c = \frac{k_f}{k_b} = \frac{[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b}$$

**Rules for writing Kc:** products on top, reactants below; each concentration (in mol/L) raised to its coefficient; concentrations are the **equilibrium** values. For gases you may use partial pressures instead → **Kp**. Pure solids and pure liquids are left out (their “concentration” is constant).
**Kc changes only with temperature** — not with concentration, pressure or a catalyst.
**Size of K:** K ≫ 1 → mostly products at equilibrium; K ≪ 1 → mostly reactants; K ≈ 1 → appreciable amounts of both.

cards.title: Reaction quotient Q: which way will it go?
body: Q is calculated exactly like K but with the concentrations **at any moment** (not necessarily at equilibrium). Compare Q with K:
**Q < K** → too little product → net reaction goes **forward (to the right)**.
**Q = K** → at equilibrium → no net change.
**Q > K** → too much product → net reaction goes **backward (to the left)**.

cards.title: Worked example: writing Kc expressions
cards.problem: Write Kc for (a) H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g); (b) 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g); (c) N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g); (d) CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g).

steps.text: (a) \(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}\)
(c) \(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{NO}_2]^2}{[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]}\)
(d) Solids are left out: \(K_c = [\text{CO}_2]\)

cards.answer: Products over reactants, powers = coefficients, no solids or pure liquids.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Le Chatelier’s Principle
body: In doing so, the system will react to restore equilibrium.

For example, if the concentration of ammonia is increased, the rate of the backward reaction will increase and more hydrogen and nitrogen will be produced, resulting in more of the ammonia being used up.
In other words the equilibrium shifts to the left until equilibrium is restored.

cards.title: Le Chatelier’s principle, step by step
body: **Le Chatelier’s principle:** if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts so as to **reduce (oppose) the stress** and reaches a new equilibrium position.
**Step 1 — Name the stress:** more or less of a substance (concentration), higher or lower pressure (volume), higher or lower temperature.
**Step 2 — Ask how the system can undo it:** use up what was added; replace what was removed; reduce a pressure increase by making fewer gas molecules.
**Step 3 — State the direction:** “shifts to the right (forward)” or “to the left (backward)”.
**Step 4 — State the result:** what happens to the amount of each substance, the colour, the yield.
**Concentration:** add a reactant or remove a product → shifts **right**; add a product or remove a reactant → shifts **left**. Kc does **not** change.

**Pressure (gases only):** count the **moles of gas** on each side. Increase pressure (decrease volume) → shift to the side with **fewer** gas moles; decrease pressure → side with **more** gas moles. Equal gas moles on both sides → **no shift**. Kc does not change.

**Also remember:** raising the temperature shifts an equilibrium in the **endothermic** direction (this *does* change K); a catalyst does **not** shift the equilibrium — it only helps reach it faster.

states.label: Equilibrium
states.text: Colourless N₂O₄ and brown NO₂ in a gas syringe at equilibrium: 1 mol gas on the left, 2 mol gas on the right.

states.label: Squeeze
states.text: Push the plunger in: half the volume, double the pressure. The gas looks darker at first (more crowded).

states.label: New equilibrium
states.text: The system reduces the pressure by forming the side with **fewer gas molecules**: 2NO₂ → N₂O₄. Fewer particles, the colour fades a little — shifted **left**.

cards.title: Model: adding N₂ to the ammonia equilibrium

steps.text: **N₂ is added**: its concentration jumps, then falls as some of it reacts — but it stays higher than before.
**H₂ is used up** with the extra N₂, so its concentration falls.
**More NH₃ forms**: the equilibrium has shifted to the **right**. Kc is the same at the new equilibrium.

cards.title: Worked example: why pressure shifts the ammonia equilibrium (using Q)
cards.problem: Show with Q why halving the volume of an equilibrium mixture of N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shifts it to the right.

steps.text: At equilibrium \(Q = K = \dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3}\).
Halving the volume **doubles** every concentration at that instant.
Q < K → the reaction goes forward (right) until Q rises back to K — more NH₃, fewer gas molecules, lower pressure.

cards.answer: Q drops to K/4, so the equilibrium shifts right.

cards.title: Worked example: predicting shifts
cards.problem: Predict the shift: (a) adding H₂ to H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g); (b) increasing pressure on the same system; (c) removing O₂ from 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃; (d) decreasing pressure on PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g).

steps.text: (a) A reactant is added → the system uses it up → shifts **right**; more HI, less I₂ (the purple colour fades).
(b) 2 gas moles on each side → **no shift** (pressure has no effect).
(c) A reactant is removed → the system replaces it → shifts **left**; SO₃ decomposes.
(d) Lower pressure → side with **more** gas moles (1 → 2) → shifts **right**; more PCl₃ and Cl₂.

cards.title: Worked example: colour changes
cards.problem: Yellow chromate turns orange dichromate in acid: 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l). What colour do you see when (a) acid is added, (b) NaOH is added?

steps.text: (a) More H⁺ (a reactant) → shift **right** → more orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ → the solution turns **orange**.
(b) OH⁻ removes H⁺ (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O) → a reactant is removed → shift **left** → more yellow CrO₄²⁻ → **yellow**.

cards.title: Memory trick
body: **“The system is stubborn — it always does the opposite.”** Add something → it uses it up. Take something away → it makes more. Squeeze it → it makes fewer gas molecules.

cards.why: Removing a product makes the system replace it → shift right → higher yield. Kc stays the same at constant temperature.

cards.title: Tips and common mistakes
body: Concentration and pressure changes move the **position**, not the **value** of K. Only temperature changes K.
Count only **gas** moles for pressure questions.
A catalyst never shifts an equilibrium.
Use the full phrase in answers: “the equilibrium shifts to the right to oppose the increase in …”.

cards.title: Reversible reactions and equilibrium
body: A **reversible reaction** can go both ways (⇌). In a closed system it reaches **dynamic equilibrium**: the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant, though both reactions are still going on.

**Le Chatelier’s principle:** if a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Example, the Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic forward reaction): increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right (fewer gas molecules, 4 → 2), so more ammonia forms; increasing the temperature shifts it to the left, so less ammonia forms.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A chemical reaction is in equilibrium when

options.B: there is change in concentration of the reactants and products.
options.C: the rate at which the reactants are used up and products produced are different.
options.D: there is no change in concentration of the reactants and products.
options.E: the quantities of reactants and products are changed.

cards.why: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. As a result, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (unchanged) over time.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: For the system $$ H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g) $$ at equilibrium, according to Le Chatelier's Principle, the reaction proceeds

options.C: forward if concentration of $$ H_2 $$ is decreased.
options.D: in neither way if pressure is increased.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the effect of pressure.**
Pressure affects equilibrium only if there is a change in the total number of moles of gas between reactants and products.

**Step 2: Count gas moles.**
- Reactants: 1 mole $$ H_2 $$ + 1 mole $$ I_2 $$ = 2 moles of gas.
- Products: 2 moles of $$ HI $$ = 2 moles of gas.

**Result:** Since the number of moles is equal on both sides ($$ 2 = 2 $$), changing the pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: For the equilibrium reaction $$ 4A(g) + B(g) \rightleftharpoons 2C(g) + 2D(g) $$, which of the following will shifts the reaction to the right:
cards.why:
According to **Le Chatelier's Principle**:
- Reactant side has $$ 4 + 1 = 5 $$ moles of gas.
- Product side has $$ 2 + 2 = 4 $$ moles of gas.
- **Increasing pressure** (or decreasing volume) shifts the equilibrium toward the side with **fewer moles** of gas (the right side).

glossary.meaning: The value Q of the equilibrium expression calculated with the concentrations at any moment; comparing Q with K shows which way the reaction will shift.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up, by providing a path with lower activation energy.
The change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time.
The state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant (dynamic equilibrium).
The rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient; it leads to the equilibrium constant Kc.

tips.text: Rate or speed refers to the amount of change in something per unit of time.
In a chemical reaction the quantity changing is the concentration of reactants and products or a certain physical property that is related to one of the concentrations.
The rate of reaction can be expressed in terms of the rate of change in concentration of either the reactants or the products.
Two conditions we impose on the reaction rate are that it must be a positive quantity, and that it must be of the same quantity regardless of the substance we use to express it.
A rate law (equation) shows us how the rate of a reaction varies with reactant concentration. But chemists also need an equation to show how reactant concentration changes with time.
This equation would allow us to summarize experimental data, which are usually reactant concentrations versus time.
We can also answer such questions as, how long will it take for a reaction to be 50 per cent complete, or what will the reactant concentration be after 5 hours.

The rate constant’s dependence on temperature can be explained by the collision theory. This theory assumes that, for a reaction to occur, reactant molecules must collide with an energy greater than a certain minimum value and with the proper orientation.
This minimum energy required for a collision between two reactant molecules, causing them to react, is called the activation energy, EA.

Some of the main factors that affect the rate of a reaction are: the temperature, the size of the particles of a solid reactant, the concentration of reactants in a solution, the pressure of reactants in the gas phase, the nature of the reactants and the presence or absence of catalyst.
Temperature: Particles fly faster → more collisions AND a bigger share clear the activation energy Ea.
Concentration / pressure: Crowded flask → more hits. For gases, squeeze the volume (higher P) does the same.
Surface area: Powder vs lump: more faces exposed. That’s why kindling lights and a log sulks.
Catalyst: New path with lower Ea. Not used up. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

questions.q: Model answer steps
questions.answer:
1. Particles gain kinetic energy.
2. They collide more often.
3. A larger fraction have E ≥ Ea so more collisions are successful.
4. Rate rises. (Don’t stop at “they move faster”.)
why: Raising the temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and, more importantly, a larger fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the rate increases.
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The effect of an increase in temperature on the rate of a reaction is to increase the  A) activation energy.  B) reactant concentration.  C) number of particle collisions.  D) energy barrier.  E) All of the above.
similar.a: C. number of particle collisions. — Temperature does not change the activation energy (energy barrier) or the concentration. Answer: C.

questions.q: A catalyst speeds a reaction by

options.B: Being used up as a reactant
options.C: Offering a path with lower Ea

why: Answer C: Offering a path with lower Ea
A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed; it is not used up and does not change ΔH.

questions.q:
Ammonia gas can be prepared in the Haber process from nitrogen and hydrogen gas as follows:
$$ N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g) \quad \Delta H = -92 \text{ KJ/mole} $$
Then large amount of ammonia is produced by:

options.A: Decreasing the temperature of the reactant
options.B: Increasing pressure on the reacting substance
options.C: Continuous addition of nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas

why:
According to **Le Chatelier's Principle**:
1. Since the reaction is **exothermic** ($$ \Delta H $$ is negative), decreasing temperature (A) shifts the equilibrium to the right.
2. Increasing pressure (B) shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (the product side).
3. Adding more reactants (C) shifts the equilibrium to the right.
Therefore, A, B, and C all increase ammonia production.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: In the reaction $$ N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g) $$. The increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium state to
why:
**Step 1:** Count the number of moles of gas on each side of the equation.
- Reactants: $$ 1 (N_2) + 3 (H_2) = 4 $$ moles of gas.
- Products: $$ 2 (NH_3) = 2 $$ moles of gas.

**Step 2:** Apply Le Chatelier's Principle.
- An increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the side with the **fewer** number of gas moles to reduce the pressure.
- Since 2 is less than 4, the equilibrium shifts to the **Right**.

**Result:** B
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The following parameters increase the rate of a reaction by increasing the rate of collision, **except**:
why:
**Step 1: Analyze how each factor affects the reaction rate.**
- **Temperature:** Increases kinetic energy, leading to more frequent and energetic collisions.
- **Concentration:** More particles in a given volume increase collision frequency.
- **Surface Area:** More exposed particles increase collision frequency.
- **Pressure:** For gases, increases particle density, increasing collision frequency.
- **Catalyst:** Increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with a **lower activation energy**, not by increasing the collision frequency.

**Result:** Catalyst is the exception.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: For a reaction $$ A + B \leftrightarrow C + \text{heat} $$, increase in temperature will increase
why:
According to **Le Chatelier's Principle**, if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the disturbance.
- The reaction is **exothermic** (heat is a product).
- Adding heat (increasing temperature) will shift the equilibrium to the **left** (the endothermic direction) to absorb the excess heat.
- Shifting left means the **backward reaction** is favored.

**Result:** B
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: For a reaction $$ \text{A} + \text{B} \leftrightarrow \text{C} + \text{heat} $$, increase in temperature will increase
why: According to Le Chatelier's Principle, for an **exothermic** reaction (where heat is a product), increasing the temperature is like adding more product. The system will shift to the left to consume the excess heat, thereby increasing the **backward reaction**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: According to the collision theory, rate of a reaction decreases when ____.
why:
According to **Collision Theory**, the rate of reaction is proportional to the frequency of effective collisions. 
- Increasing pressure, surface area, concentration, or temperature all **increase** the rate. 
- Increasing **particle size** (e.g., using a large lump instead of powder) **decreases** the surface area, which leads to fewer collisions and a **decreased** reaction rate.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Consider the reaction: $$ 2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2H_2O_{(g)} \quad \Delta H = -483.6 kJ $$. Which of the following is true about the reaction?

options.A: Increasing temperature will shift the equilibrium to the left.
options.B: Increasing pressure will shift the equilibrium to the left.
options.C: Increasing Volume will not have any effect on the equilibrium.
options.D: Increasing concentration of O2(g) will shift the equilibrium to the left

why:
**Step 1: Temperature.** The reaction is exothermic ($$ \Delta H < 0 $$). According to Le Chatelier's Principle, increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the endothermic direction (left). (True)
**Step 2: Pressure.** Reactant moles = 3, Product moles = 2. Increasing pressure shifts to the side with fewer moles (right). (False)
**Step 3: Concentration.** Increasing $$ O_2 $$ (reactant) shifts equilibrium to the product side (right). (False).
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The rate of reaction is increased by the following, except;

options.C: Increasing the size of the particle

why:
**Step 1:** Review factors that increase reaction rate.
- **Temp:** Increases kinetic energy and collisions (Increases rate).
- **Conc:** More particles per volume, more collisions (Increases rate).
- **Catalyst:** Lowers activation energy (Increases rate).
- **Surface Area:** More area for collisions (Increases rate).
**Step 2:** **Increasing particle size** actually **decreases** the surface area. Therefore, it **decreases** the rate of reaction.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: For the decomposition of $$ SO_3 $$ to form $$ SO_2 $$ and $$ O_2 $$, $$ K_c $$ is $$ 2.43 \times 10^{-3} $$ at $$ 273 ^\circ\text{C} $$. Then what is the $$ K_c $$ for the **reverse reaction**?
why:
The equilibrium constant for a reverse reaction ($$ K' $$) is the reciprocal of the equilibrium constant for the forward reaction ($$ K $$).
$$ K' = 1 / K $$
$$ K' = 1 / (2.43 \times 10^{-3}) $$
$$ K' \approx 411.52 \approx 4.12 \times 10^2 $$.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: All of the following factors affect the industrial preparation of ammonia, **except**
why: The industrial preparation of ammonia (Haber process) is an equilibrium reaction: $$ N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3 $$. According to Le Chatelier's principle, it is affected by temperature, pressure, and concentration. A catalyst increases the rate. **Light** does not significantly affect this specific gaseous reaction.

questions.q: For a reaction Kc = 4.0. A mixture has Qc = 10. In which direction will the reaction proceed? Explain.
questions.answer: To the left (backward), because Qc > Kc: there is too much product.
why: Step 1: compare Q with K: 10 > 4.0.
Step 2: Q > K means the ratio products/reactants is too large.
Step 3: the backward reaction is faster until Q falls to 4.0.
questions.tip: Q < K → right; Q > K → left.
